did_you_know.text: Did you know? Psalm 32 opens with the word “Blessed” and presents forgiveness as a great blessing: “Blessed is the one whose transgression is forgiven and whose sin is covered.”
Did you know? The verse describes inner integrity as accompanying true happiness: the happy person is one to whom the Lord does not charge iniquity and in whose spirit there is no deceit.
Did you know? The psalmist describes concealing sin through physical imagery: his bones waste away, and he groans all day long. In this way, the text presents silence as a source of deep suffering.
Did you know? The Lord’s “hand” is described as heavy upon the psalmist day and night, and his strength dries up “as in the heat of summer”—an image of heat, dryness, and a sense of wasting away.

Did you know? The turning point in the psalm is confession: the psalmist acknowledges his sin, does not conceal his iniquity, and confesses his transgressions; as a result, he describes the iniquity as being taken away from him.

Did you know? After describing personal confession, the psalm broadens its message to every “godly person”: prayer to the Lord is presented as a response in times of distress, before the floods of mighty waters reach him.
Did you know? The psalmist calls the Lord his “hiding place”—a place of refuge—and describes Him both as a protection from trouble and as one who surrounds him with songs of deliverance.

Did you know? This verse uses the language of personal guidance: “I will instruct you and teach you.” This guidance includes learning, instruction, and counsel, and is described as watchful care through “my eye.”

Did you know? The horse and the mule serve here as a metaphor for a person without understanding: just as an animal needs a bit and bridle to come near, so people are called to act with understanding rather than merely under external compulsion.

Did you know? The psalm draws a sharp contrast between the many “pains” of the wicked and the steadfast love surrounding the one who trusts in the Lord; it concludes by calling the righteous and upright in heart to rejoice, be glad, and sing for joy.
